inline_text:
This follows up on the discussion in #8, where @jordanauge invited suggestions as PRs. It turns my earlier comment on §9.4 into a concrete paragraph so it can be discussed, reworded or moved.

The PR targets the `d1` branch rather than `main`, because the D1 chapters only exist in #8 for now. That way it can be read against the current text and folded into #8 if it is useful. If retargeting to `main` after #8 lands is easier, I'm happy to do that.

The change is one paragraph in §9.4, next to the dashboard reporting fields. When a panel or report claims coverage or defect-detection effectiveness, it asks for the counting unit and declared inventory, the selected subset, what was exercised, and what was excluded or could not complete, and it asks that items which were not exercised be reported as such rather than silently folded into another count. For mutation results it keeps detected, exercised but undetected, and never exercised defects apart, and asks for timeouts, errors and equivalent mutants to be named rather than merged. §1.3 says that for benchmark inventories and coverage matrices "the minimum vocabulary and required reporting fields those artifacts should use are defined", and this paragraph applies the same idea to coverage and defect-detection claims on a panel. No new score, threshold or tool requirement is introduced. I used "seeded defects" rather than "faults" so it does not collide with the infrastructure faults behind fault robustness in §5 and §9.2.

Compared with my comment, the paragraph is both trimmed and extended. Mainly, out went the changed implementation and fixed test set, the specific assertion that detected a change, the note on reporting instrument controls separately, the four baseline tests in the example, and the literature on AI-generated tests. New are the three groups for mutation results, the rule about items that were not exercised, the wider scope (scenarios and failure modes as well as tests), and the guidance on naming timeouts, errors and equivalent mutants.

That last part comes from how two mutation tools, Stryker and PIT, treat those outcomes. Stryker's [mutant states and metrics](https://stryker-mutator.io/docs/mutation-testing-elements/mutant-states-and-metrics/) page counts a timeout as detected and leaves runtime errors, compile errors and ignored mutants out of the mutation score. PIT's [`DetectionStatus`](https://github.com/hcoles/pitest/blob/d7c2531999e0aaff2b096c5a54bc071a99df30e8/pitest/src/main/java/org/pitest/mutationtest/DetectionStatus.java) enum marks timed out, non-viable, memory error, run error and equivalent mutants as detected, and its [`MutationStatistics`](https://github.com/hcoles/pitest/blob/d7c2531999e0aaff2b096c5a54bc071a99df30e8/pitest-entry/src/main/java/org/pitest/mutationtest/statistics/MutationStatistics.java) reports the detected share of all mutants. An errored mutant can therefore drop out of one tool's score and count as detected in the other's, which is why the paragraph asks for the groups rather than a single number.

Any of the trimmed parts can go back in, and the paragraph can just as easily be shortened further or moved to §10 if it reads better there.

AI assisted and carefully adjusted
